course_information.title: Outdoor Power Equipment Fundamentals
course_information.description: Recognize common outdoor power equipment, gather customer needs, compare power sources, and use manufacturer guidance for safe product consultation.
course_information.scope: General independent hardware retail; not store-specific
course_information.restrictions: Retail product consultation only. No pesticide application certification, hazardous repair procedures, or tree work instruction.
learning_objectives: Identify common outdoor power equipment and intended tasks.
Compare battery, corded, and engine-powered options using product specifications.
Ask questions about equipment size, capacity, and accessories.
Explain basic maintenance and storage questions using manufacturer instructions.
Recognize safety concerns and refer service or repairs to trained professionals.

lessons.title: Recognize Common Outdoor Power Equipment
lessons.objective: Match broad equipment categories to customer jobs.
lessons.why_this_matters: A customer may know the task but not the tool name.

content.heading: Equipment families
content.text: Mowers cut grass. String trimmers cut grass near obstacles. Edgers define edges. Blowers move loose debris. Hedge trimmers shape hedges. Chainsaws cut wood within their intended use.

content.heading: Ask about the job
content.text: Find out the material, area size, terrain, and frequency of use. A tool built for a small residential task may not suit a large property or heavy use.

content.heading: Respect operating limits
content.text: Every machine has intended uses and restrictions. Do not suggest removing guards, defeating safety devices, or using attachments the manufacturer has not approved.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer says they need something to clear grass around fence posts. Ask whether they mean grass trimming or edging before showing options.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “What are you cutting, and where will you use the machine?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Recommending a chainsaw for trimming grass; confusing a string trimmer with a hedge trimmer.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer unclear or hazardous cutting tasks to an experienced equipment specialist.

lessons.title: Compare Battery, Corded, and Engine Power
lessons.objective: Explain basic power-source tradeoffs without making promises.
lessons.why_this_matters: Power source affects convenience, runtime, noise, upkeep, and where equipment can be used.

content.heading: Battery equipment
content.text: Battery tools need a compatible battery and charger. Runtime depends on the model, battery, workload, and conditions. Batteries are not necessarily interchangeable between brands or systems.

content.heading: Corded equipment
content.text: Corded tools require a suitable electrical supply and properly rated cords when allowed by the manufacturer. The cord limits range and introduces trip and damage hazards.

content.heading: Engine equipment
content.text: Gasoline-powered equipment has fuel, exhaust, noise, and maintenance requirements. Never operate combustion-engine equipment indoors or in enclosed spaces due to carbon monoxide risk.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a blower for a small patio and asks if any battery will fit. Explain that compatibility must be verified for the specific tool system.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s check the model, compatible battery, and expected use.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Claiming every battery fits every tool; promising a fixed runtime for all conditions.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a specialist about battery compatibility, charging faults, fuel requirements, or electrical supply questions.

lessons.title: Match Equipment to the Customer’s Property
lessons.objective: Gather practical specifications before recommending a model.
lessons.why_this_matters: The wrong size or feature set can make a job difficult or unsafe.

content.heading: Measure the job
content.text: Ask about property size, slope, obstacles, storage space, and how often the equipment will be used. Avoid promising that one machine suits every yard.

content.heading: Compare relevant features
content.text: For mowers, compare cutting width and manufacturer-approved terrain limitations. For blowers, look at the published performance specifications and intended application. For saws, do not treat bar length alone as a measure of safe capability.

content.heading: Confirm accessories
content.text: Check which batteries, chargers, cutting attachments, protective equipment, and replacement parts are included or sold separately. Use the manufacturer’s compatibility list.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a mower for a sloped yard. Ask about the slope and compare only models whose manuals support the intended conditions.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “How large is the area? Is it flat or sloped? Are there gates or tight spaces?”
lessons.common_mistakes: Choosing by horsepower or price alone; ignoring slope limitations and included accessories.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate steep terrain, large trees, overhead hazards, and unclear equipment limits.

lessons.title: Explain Maintenance and Storage Safely
lessons.objective: Direct customers to model-specific care instructions.
lessons.why_this_matters: Correct maintenance helps equipment work reliably and prevents avoidable hazards.

content.heading: Start with the manual
content.text: Maintenance varies by engine, battery system, and tool model. Refer to the operator manual for cleaning, inspection, service intervals, and approved parts.

content.heading: Storage matters
content.text: Customers should follow manufacturer guidance for battery storage, fuel handling, and seasonal storage. Never invent a fuel mix ratio or recommend storing fuel near heat or ignition sources.

content.heading: Know your role
content.text: Retail employees may help locate approved parts and manuals. Repairs, blade servicing, and other hazardous work should be handled by trained authorized personnel as appropriate.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks what fuel mixture to use in a trimmer. Ask for the exact model and check the manufacturer manual instead of giving a universal ratio.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Fuel requirements vary. Let’s verify the exact model instructions before you add anything.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming all two-stroke engines use the same fuel ratio; handling sharp blades without training.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer repairs, battery damage, leaking fuel, and complex maintenance to trained service personnel.

choices.text: Check the exact model and manual
Tell them all machines use straight gasoline

lessons.title: Recognize Equipment Safety and Service Limits
lessons.objective: Explain safety boundaries and escalate hazardous situations.
lessons.why_this_matters: Outdoor power tools can cause serious injuries when used incorrectly.

content.heading: Personal protection
content.text: Manufacturer instructions may require eye, hearing, hand, foot, or other protection depending on the machine. Follow the specific manual and store policy.

content.heading: Keep guards in place
content.text: Do not recommend bypassing interlocks, removing guards, using damaged batteries, or operating a tool with a missing safety component.

content.heading: Escalate risky work
content.text: Tree work near power lines, damaged electrical equipment, unstable slopes, fuel leaks, and active mechanical faults are not routine retail consultations. Direct customers to qualified professionals and appropriate emergency help when needed.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks how to disable a mower safety switch that keeps stopping the engine. Decline to give bypass instructions and refer them to authorized service.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “That safety device must stay functional. Let’s find the approved service option.”
lessons.common_mistakes: Giving instructions to defeat a guard or switch; offering unverified repair steps.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate immediately when there is leaking fuel, a swollen battery, an electrical hazard, or unsafe cutting conditions.
